# TCB Allowed List — Nanvix phys-mm

Any `external_body` outside this list must be removed.

## Allowed `external_body`

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::instance` — materializes a `&'static mut Inner` from the
  module-level `static mut INSTANCE: MaybeUninit<Inner>` singleton (guarded by `INSTANCE_INIT`).
  Raw-memory op over externally-owned `static mut` storage Verus cannot verify without a
  `PointsTo` (mirrors `bump_allocator`/`raw-array`). `ensures` pins the singleton's abstract
  state to `phys_view().frames`, asserts `(*r).inv()`, and records `phys_view().initialized` —
  the §8 ghost-token attachment for the singleton frame allocator.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::deref`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::deref_mut`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::clear`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::new` — wraps a `FrameAddress` into an owning
  kernel-frame handle. Its body calls `crate::mm::virt::identity_map_page`, whose precondition is
  the **global** `identity_map_view().inv()`. That fact is owned by the `mm::virt` identity-map
  ghost token (a parameter-free singleton-global, like `phys_view()`), which is not realized in the
  `mm::phys` module and cannot be derived from the only available precondition (`base.inv()`). So
  the body cannot discharge the callee's `requires` in-scope. Same cross-module global-token
  deferral as `frame::book`/`frame::alloc` (post-mutation `phys_view()`): `external_body` until
  `mm::virt`'s identity-map token is realized, at which point `new` can pass it to
  `identity_map_page` and be verified in-body. `ensures Ok(kf) => kf@ == base@ && kf.inv()` (the
  address is preserved and page-aligned); `kframe`'s siblings `base`/`drop` verify in-body.
- `src/libs/bump_allocator/src/lib.rs::FixedSizeBumpAllocator::alloc` — materializes a
  `&'static mut [u8; N]` from a backend-provided address (`usize as *mut`); raw-memory
  op Verus cannot verify without a `PointsTo` for the externally-owned `BssStorage`
  region. Mirrors `src/libs/raw-array`. `ensures` states alignment + in-bounds over
  the abstract `bump_view`.
- `src/libs/bump_allocator/src/lib.rs::FixedSizeBumpAllocator::alloc_as` — delegates to
  `alloc` and re-materializes the slot as `&'static mut MaybeUninit<T>`; same rationale.
  `ensures` adds the `size_of::<T>()`/`align_of::<T>()` vs `(N, A)` guard arms.

## `external_body` introduced while speccing `arch::x86::mem::paging::table`

- `src/libs/arch/src/x86/mem/paging/table.rs::Table::<E>::read` — reads a `TableEntry` from a
  page-table slot through a raw pointer materialized from `self.base` (`usize as *const E::Word`).
  Verus does not support `usize`→pointer casts (int-to-ptr materialization of externally-owned,
  volatile page-table memory), so the body cannot be verified. Same trust-boundary rationale as
  `bump_allocator::alloc` (`usize as *mut`) and `frame::instance`. See
  `nanvix-phys-arch-paging-table/verus-unsupported.md`. **The function is not contract-free:** it
  carries a full `#[verus_spec]` pinned to the global page-table-memory ghost — `requires index@ <
  PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH`, `ensures result == spec_table_read::<E>(self@.addr, index@)` — exactly as
  `frame::instance` pins its result to `phys_view()` (parameter-free global ghost, no signature
  change).
- `src/libs/arch/src/x86/mem/paging/table.rs::Table::<E>::write` — writes a `TableEntry` into a
  page-table slot through a raw pointer materialized from `self.base` (`usize as *mut E::Word`).
  Same int-to-ptr / volatile externally-owned-memory limitation as `read`. Carries only the sound
  `requires index@ < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH` (auto from `TableIndex::inv`); it has **no** contents

## `assume_specification` for not-yet-verified callees (eliminated when their module is verified)

Most of these `assume_specification` (and one `external_type_specification`) declarations live
in `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.spec.rs`; a few co-locate with the type they describe (the
`PageAligned` ones now live in `src/kernel/src/hal/mem/types/address/aligned/page.spec.rs`,
per the comment at `page.spec.rs:26-37`). They give trusted contracts to callees of the (now
verified-in-body) `Inner` frame-allocator methods so those bodies translate. Each is superseded
by the real specification when its module is verified — the same "superseded when the address
layer is verified" rationale already used for `FrameAddress::from_raw_value`/`into_raw_value`.

- **External crate (`arch`) — genuinely outside the kernel crate, temporary placeholder:**
  - `::arch::mem::paging::FrameNumber` — `external_type_specification` (`ExFrameNumber`).
  - `::arch::mem::FRAME_SIZE` — `ensures result == spec_page_size()`.
  - `::arch::mem::paging::FrameNumber::from_raw_value` / `into_raw_value`.
  - `::arch::mem::PAGE_ALIGNMENT` — declared at
    `src/kernel/src/hal/mem/types/address/aligned/page.spec.rs:7`. `PAGE_ALIGNMENT` is a
    `pub const Alignment` in the external `arch` crate (`Alignment::Align4096`), declared
    outside any `verus!` block, so Verus cannot resolve its value and exec code referencing
    it has no specification (removing the declaration fails to compile with
    `error: cannot use function arch::x86::mem::constants::PAGE_ALIGNMENT which is ignored
    because it is either declared outside the verus! macro or marked as external`). Trusted
    contract: `ensures ::sys::mm::spec_align_value(result) == spec_page_size()` — it pins the
    arch alignment's numeric value to `spec_page_size()`, the link `from_address` relies on to

4. //==================================================================================================
5. // Imports
6. //==================================================================================================
7. 
8. use vstd::prelude::*;
9. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
10. include!("table.spec.rs");
11. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
12. include!("table.proof.rs");
13. 
14. use super::{
15.     PteWord,
16.     PTE_WORD_SIZE_LOG2,
17. };
18. 
19. //==================================================================================================
20. // Table Entry Trait
21. //==================================================================================================
22. 
23. ///
24. /// # Description
25. ///
26. /// Trait bound for entry types that can be stored in a page table.
27. ///
28. /// The raw representation uses [`PteWord`] — `u32` on x86.
29. ///
30. #[verus_verify]
31. pub trait TableEntry: Copy {
32.     /// Creates from a raw [`PteWord`], returning `None` if the value is invalid.
33.     #[verus_spec(result =>
34.         ensures result == spec_entry_from_raw::<Self>(raw),
35.     )]
36.     fn from_raw(raw: PteWord) -> Option<Self>;
37.     /// Returns the raw [`PteWord`] representation.
38.     #[verus_spec(result =>
39.         ensures result == spec_entry_raw(self),
40.     )]
41.     fn raw(self) -> PteWord;
42. }
43. 
44. //==================================================================================================
45. // Table Index
46. //==================================================================================================
47. 
48. ///
49. /// # Description
50. ///
51. /// A validated index into a page table, guaranteed to be in `[0, PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH)`.
52. ///
53. #[verus_verify]
54. #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
55. pub struct TableIndex(usize);
56. 
57. #[verus_verify]
58. impl TableIndex {
59.     ///
60.     /// # Description
61.     ///
62.     /// Creates a [`TableIndex`] from a raw `usize`, returning `None` if the value is out of
63.     /// bounds.
64.     ///
65.     #[verus_spec(result =>
66.         ensures
67.             match result {
68.                 Some(t) => index < crate::mem::PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH && t@ == index as nat,
69.                 None => index >= crate::mem::PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH,
70.             },
71.     )]
72.     pub const fn new(index: usize) -> Option<Self> {
73.         if index < crate::mem::PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH {
74.             Some(Self(index))
75.         } else {
76.             None
77.         }
78.     }
79. 
80.     ///
81.     /// # Description
82.     ///
83.     /// Returns the underlying index value.
84.     ///
85.     #[verus_spec(result =>
86.         ensures
87.             result as nat == self@,
88.             result < crate::mem::PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH,
89.     )]
90.     pub const fn into_raw(self) -> usize {
91.         proof! { use_type_invariant(self); }
92.         self.0
93.     }
94. }
95. 
96. //==================================================================================================
97. // Virtual Address Index Extraction
98. //==================================================================================================
99. 
100. /// Extracts the PD index (bits 22-31) from a virtual address as a [`TableIndex`].
101. #[verus_spec(result =>
102.     ensures
103.         result@ == spec_pd_index(vaddr),
104.         result@ < crate::mem::PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH,
105. )]
106. pub const fn pd_index(vaddr: usize) -> TableIndex {
107.     proof! { assert(crate::mem::PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH == 1024) by (compute); }
108.     // The mask guarantees the result is always < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH.
109.     let index: usize = (vaddr >> crate::mem::PGTAB_SHIFT) & (crate::mem::PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH - 1);
110.     proof! {
111.         assert(crate::mem::PGTAB_SHIFT == 22) by (compute);
112.         assert(index < 1024) by (bit_vector)
113.             requires index == (vaddr >> 22usize) & 1023usize;
114.     }
115.     TableIndex(index)
116. }
117. 
118. /// Extracts the PT index (bits 12-21) from a virtual address as a [`TableIndex`].
119. #[verus_spec(result =>
120.     ensures
121.         result@ == spec_pt_index(vaddr),
122.         result@ < crate::mem::PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH,
123. )]
124. pub const fn pt_index(vaddr: usize) -> TableIndex {
125.     proof! { assert(crate::mem::PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH == 1024) by (compute); }
126.     // The mask guarantees the result is always < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH.
127.     let index: usize = (vaddr >> crate::mem::PAGE_SHIFT) & (crate::mem::PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH - 1);
128.     proof! {
129.         assert(crate::mem::PAGE_SHIFT == 12) by (compute);
130.         assert(index < 1024) by (bit_vector)
131.             requires index == (vaddr >> 12usize) & 1023usize;
132.     }
133.     TableIndex(index)
134. }
135. 
136. //==================================================================================================
137. // Table
138. //==================================================================================================
139. 
140. ///
141. /// # Description
142. ///
143. /// A page-table page containing [`PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH`](crate::mem::PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH) entries.
144. ///
145. /// This type is parameterized over the entry type to enforce that each table level uses only
146. /// its own entry kind (e.g., PD tables only [`PageDirectoryEntry`], PT tables only
147. /// [`PageTableEntry`]).
148. ///
149. /// The table is accessed via a base address that must be valid in the current address space
150. /// (i.e., a mapped virtual address). It does not own the backing memory — the caller is
151. /// responsible for allocation and lifetime management.
152. ///
153. #[verus_verify]
154. #[derive(Debug)]
155. pub struct Table<E: TableEntry> {
156.     /// Base address of the table (must be page-aligned).
157.     base: usize,
158.     /// Phantom marker for the entry type.
159.     _marker: ::core::marker::PhantomData<E>,
160. }
161. 
162. #[verus_verify]
163. impl<E: TableEntry> Table<E> {
164.     ///
165.     /// # Description
166.     ///
167.     /// Creates a table reference from a base address.
168.     ///
169.     /// # Safety
170.     ///
171.     /// `base` must be a valid, page-aligned address with at least one page of readable/writable
172.     /// memory.
173.     ///
174.     #[verus_spec(result =>
175.         ensures result@.addr == base as nat,
176.     )]
177.     pub const unsafe fn from_address(base: usize) -> Self {
178.         Self {
179.             base,
180.             _marker: ::core::marker::PhantomData,
181.         }
182.     }
183. 
184.     ///
185.     /// # Description
186.     ///
187.     /// Reads the entry at `index`.
188.     ///
189.     /// Returns `None` if the raw value is invalid according to `E::from_raw()`.
190.     ///
191.     /// # Safety
192.     ///
193.     /// The memory at `base + index * size_of::<PteWord>()` must be valid for a volatile read.
194.     ///
195.     // Trust boundary (see `verus-ai-logs/.../tcb-allowed.md` and `verus-unsupported.md`):
196.     // materializes a raw `*const PteWord` from the integer base address (`usize as *const`) and
197.     // performs a volatile load — the hardware page-table access. Verus does not support the
198.     // `usize -> *const T` cast, so the body cannot be verified; this mirrors the
199.     // `bump_allocator::alloc` / `frame::instance` int-to-pointer materialization boundaries.
200.     // The `ensures` pins the (trusted) result to the global page-table memory ghost, exactly as
201.     // `frame::instance` pins its result to `phys_view()` — no exec signature change.
202.     #[verus_verify(external_body)]
203.     #[verus_spec(result =>
204.         requires
205.             index@ < crate::mem::PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH,
206.         ensures
207.             result == spec_table_read::<E>(self@.addr, index@),
208.     )]
209.     pub unsafe fn read(&self, index: TableIndex) -> Option<E> {
210.         let offset: usize = index.into_raw() << PTE_WORD_SIZE_LOG2;
211.         let ptr: *const PteWord = (self.base + offset) as *const PteWord;
212.         E::from_raw(::core::ptr::read_volatile(ptr))
213.     }
214. 
215.     ///
216.     /// # Description
217.     ///
218.     /// Writes `entry` at `index`.
219.     ///
220.     /// # Safety
221.     ///
222.     /// The memory at `base + index * size_of::<PteWord>()` must be valid for a volatile write.
223.     ///
224.     // Trust boundary (see `tcb-allowed.md` / `verus-unsupported.md`): materializes a raw
225.     // `*mut PteWord` from the integer base address and performs a volatile store — the hardware
226.     // page-table write. The `usize -> *mut T` cast is unsupported by Verus, so the body cannot be
227.     // verified; same int-to-pointer boundary as `read`.
228.     //
229.     // No contents `ensures`: page-table memory is *mutable* volatile state, but `write` takes
230.     // `&self` and the global ghost `spec_table_word(addr, index)` is a *pure* function (one fixed
231.     // value per slot). Pinning that pure cell to the caller-chosen `entry` in an `external_body`
232.     // (hence *assumed*) postcondition is unsound — two writes of distinct entries to the same slot
233.     // would assume `spec_entry_raw(e1) == spec_entry_raw(e2)`, and with `lemma_entry_roundtrip`
234.     // that derives `e1 == e2`, i.e. `false`. The slot-update transition
235.     // (`self@.entries[index@] == Some(entry)` after the call, with all other slots framed) is a
236.     // genuine `old@ -> @` state change and is therefore *deferred to the proving-phase page-table
237.     // permission token* — exactly the deferral convention used by `identity_map_view()`'s
238.     // `v -> v'` in `identity_map.spec.rs` (a global accessor whose cross-call transition is
239.     // realized later by a ghost token, "not a verification escape"). Only the sound `requires`
240.     // (in-range index, auto from `TableIndex::inv`) is kept here.
241.     #[verus_verify(external_body)]
242.     #[verus_spec(
243.         requires
244.             index@ < crate::mem::PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH,
245.     )]
246.     pub unsafe fn write(&self, index: TableIndex, entry: E) {
247.         let offset: usize = index.into_raw() << PTE_WORD_SIZE_LOG2;
248.         let ptr: *mut PteWord = (self.base + offset) as *mut PteWord;
249.         ::core::ptr::write_volatile(ptr, entry.raw());
250.     }
251. }
252.

3. //==================================================================================================
4. // TableIndex — a validated page-table slot number
5. //==================================================================================================
6. 
7. // A `TableIndex` carries exactly one piece of caller-visible information: the validated index
8. // value. Its abstract value is a single `nat` (see `view_design.md`).
9. impl View for TableIndex {
10.     type V = nat;
11. 
12.     // `closed`: callers reference `self@` and the in-range invariant; the mapping to the inner
13.     // `usize` field is hidden. The abstract value is "the validated slot number".
14.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> nat {
15.         self.0 as nat
16.     }
17. }
18. 
19. impl TableIndex {
20.     // The validated-range guarantee every caller depends on: a `TableIndex` is always a legal
21.     // slot. Enforced as a type invariant so the bound holds unconditionally for any value callers
22.     // hold — this is exactly what keeps `read`/`write` (and `gva.rs`'s `checked_mul`) within one
23.     // page, and is established once at each construction site (`new`, `pd_index`, `pt_index`).
24.     #[verifier::type_invariant]
25.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
26.         self@ < crate::mem::PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH
27.     }
28. }
29. 
30. //==================================================================================================
31. // Virtual-address index extraction (pure helpers)
32. //==================================================================================================
33. 
34. // Low `log2(PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH)` bits of `vaddr >> shift`. Mirrors the exec masking
35. // `(vaddr >> shift) & (PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH - 1)` exactly; the mask makes the result `< LEN`.
36. pub open spec fn spec_table_index(vaddr: usize, shift: usize) -> nat {
37.     ((vaddr >> shift) & ((crate::mem::PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH - 1) as usize)) as nat
38. }
39. 
40. // PD index = bits [PGTAB_SHIFT, PGTAB_SHIFT + log2(LEN)) of `vaddr`.
41. pub open spec fn spec_pd_index(vaddr: usize) -> nat {
42.     spec_table_index(vaddr, crate::mem::PGTAB_SHIFT)
43. }
44. 
45. // PT index = bits [PAGE_SHIFT, PAGE_SHIFT + log2(LEN)) of `vaddr`.
46. pub open spec fn spec_pt_index(vaddr: usize) -> nat {
47.     spec_table_index(vaddr, crate::mem::PAGE_SHIFT)
48. }
49. 
50. //==================================================================================================
51. // TableEntry codec (the per-entry round-trip law)
52. //==================================================================================================
53. 
54. // Abstract serialization / decoding of a `TableEntry`. These mirror the exec `raw` / `from_raw`
55. // trait methods. They are deliberately *unbounded* over `E` (no `TableEntry` bound) to avoid a
56. // definitional cycle (`TableEntry`'s method specs reference these, so a bound here would make the
57. // trait depend on a function that depends on the trait).
58. //
59. // `spec_entry_from_raw` returns `None` for a word that is not a valid encoding of `E` — exactly
60. // the `read` failure path callers map to `InvalidArgument` (see `caller_analysis.md`).
61. pub uninterp spec fn spec_entry_raw<E>(e: E) -> PteWord;
62. 
63. pub uninterp spec fn spec_entry_from_raw<E>(w: PteWord) -> Option<E>;
64. 
65. //==================================================================================================
66. // Global ghost model of page-table memory
67. //==================================================================================================
68. 
69. // Page-table memory is volatile, caller-owned storage the `Table<E>` handle does not contain
70. // (the struct holds only `base`). It is modeled here as a *global, parameter-free* ghost
71. // function — the same device used for the physical-frame subsystem (`mm::phys::phys_view()`):
72. // the abstract state is named globally rather than threaded through a permission parameter, so
73. // `read`/`write` keep their exec signatures and do not cascade ghost arguments into out-of-scope
74. // callers (`identity_map::ensure_pt`/`ensure_pte`/`identity_map_page`).
75. //
76. // `spec_table_word(addr, index)` is the raw word currently stored at slot `index` of the
77. // page-table page based at `addr`. Because it is a pure function, a call to `write` only updates
78. // knowledge about the *one* slot named in its `ensures`; every other slot/page is automatically
79. // preserved across the call (the caller-facing frame condition). The cross-call write transition
80. // (and its consistency when the same slot is written twice) is realized in the proving phase by a
81. // ghost token over the page-table pages — exactly the `phys_view()` "transition realized in the
82. // proving phase" placeholder.
83. pub uninterp spec fn spec_table_word(addr: nat, index: nat) -> PteWord;
84. 
85. // The decoded entry currently stored at slot `index` of the page based at `addr`: the value a
86. // `read` returns. This is the `index -> Option<E>` entry map from `view_design.md`, expressed
87. // pointwise over the global word store.
88. pub open spec fn spec_table_read<E>(addr: nat, index: nat) -> Option<E> {
89.     spec_entry_from_raw::<E>(spec_table_word(addr, index))
90. }
91. 
92. //==================================================================================================
93. // Table<E> — a typed, non-owning handle over one page-table page
94. //==================================================================================================
95. 
96. // To callers a `Table<E>` is a typed handle over the page at a physical/identity-mapped base
97. // address (see `view_design.md`): its caller-meaningful identity is *which page* read/write act
98. // on (`addr`), and its observable contents are the per-slot decoded entry map (`entries`). The
99. // contents live in volatile, caller-owned memory the struct does not store, so the view reads
100. // them from the global `spec_table_read` ghost rather than from struct fields.
101. pub struct TableView<E> {
102.     /// Physical/identity-mapped base address this handle denotes.
103.     pub addr: nat,
104.     /// Decoded entry at each valid slot — `entries[i]` is what `read(i)` returns
105.     /// (`None` = the slot holds a word that is not a valid encoding of `E`).
106.     pub entries: Map<nat, Option<E>>,
107. }
108. 
109. impl<E: TableEntry> View for Table<E> {
110.     type V = TableView<E>;
111. 
112.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> TableView<E> {
113.         TableView {
114.             addr: self.base as nat,
115.             entries: Map::new(
116.                 |i: nat| i < crate::mem::PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH,
117.                 |i: nat| spec_table_read::<E>(self.base as nat, i),
118.             ),
119.         }
120.     }
121. }
122. 
123. } // verus!

1. # Caller Analysis: `arch::x86::mem::paging::table`
2. 
3. ## Script Output
4. 
5. Raw `find_callers_lsp.py` output reported **7 public exec functions, 0 private,
6. 2 types (`Table`, `TableIndex`)** and — importantly — **0 external callers for
7. every public function** (only internal callers of `TableIndex::into_raw` from
8. `Table::read`/`Table::write`).
9. 
10. > **Why the script found 0 external callers (false negative).**
11. > This module lives under `src/libs/arch/src/x86/` — the **32-bit x86** build.
12. > rust-analyzer (and thus the script) indexes the **x86_64 host** configuration,
13. > so all real call sites — which are compiled only under `cfg(target_arch =
14. > "x86")` (kernel) or are host-side software page-walkers — are invisible to the
15. > LSP. A textual search across the workspace recovers the true callers below.
16. > Treat the script's "no external callers" warning as a configuration artifact,
17. > **not** as evidence of dead code.
18. 
19. In-scope (verification-order) functions: `Table::write`, `TableIndex::into_raw`,
20. `raw`, `Table::read`, `from_raw`, `pt_index`, `TableIndex`, `pd_index`,
21. `Table::from_address`. (`raw`/`from_raw` are the `TableEntry` trait methods,
22. implemented in `pde.rs`/`pte.rs` and dispatched only inside `Table::read`/`write`.)
23. 
24. ## Real Callers (recovered by source search)
25. 
26. ### 1. Kernel identity map — `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/identity_map.rs` (primary consumer)
27. 
28. This is the canonical user of the whole module. It walks/builds the kernel's
29. two-level identity map:
30. 
31. - `paging::pd_index(vaddr)` / `paging::pt_index(vaddr)` → `TableIndex`
32.   (L131, L306, L728, L729, L783, L848).
33. - `unsafe { Table::<PageDirectoryEntry>::from_address(pd_paddr) }` and
34.   `Table::<PageTableEntry>::from_address(pt_paddr)` to obtain a typed view over a
35.   physical (identity-mapped) page (L133, L297, L299, L732, L736, L785, L852, L863).
36. - `unsafe { pd.read(pde_idx) }` / `pt.read(pte_idx)` returning
37.   `Option<PageDirectoryEntry>` / `Option<PageTableEntry>`; callers treat `None`
38.   as "invalid entry" → `ErrorCode::InvalidArgument` (L308, L316, L535, L633,
39.   L786, L853, L864).
40. - `unsafe { pd.write(pde_idx, new_pde) }` / `pt.write(pte_idx, new_pte)` to
41.   install freshly-built entries (L320, L583, L665).
42. - The entry-type parameter `E` is fixed per level: PD tables only carry
43.   `PageDirectoryEntry`, PT tables only `PageTableEntry`. The phantom-typed
44.   `Table<E>` is exactly what enforces this at the call sites.
45. 
46. ### 2. UserVM guest page walker — `src/uservm/src/guest_profiler/gva.rs` (host-side)
47. 
48. `translate_gva()` performs a *software* two-level walk over guest memory:
49. 
50. ```rust
51. let pd_index: usize = paging::pd_index(gva as usize).into_raw();
52. let pt_index: usize = paging::pt_index(gva as usize).into_raw();
53. ```
54. 
55. Here only `pd_index`/`pt_index` and `TableIndex::into_raw` are used; the table
56. bytes are read directly from a host pointer (`read_unaligned`) rather than via
57. `Table::read`, because the guest's memory is not mapped into the host address
58. space. This caller relies *solely* on the index-extraction arithmetic being
59. correct (mask to `[0, PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH)`) and on `into_raw` returning that same
60. value unchanged.
61. 
62. ## Pre-existing Specs (from upstream verification)
63. 
64. - **Source:** added while verifying the kernel `mm::virt::identity_map` module.
65. - **File:** `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/identity_map.spec.rs`.
66. - These are **trusted external boundary specs** for this not-yet-verified module:
67.   - `#[verifier::external_type_specification] #[external_body]` for
68.     `Table<E>` (`ExTable`) and `TableIndex` (`ExTableIndex`) — both opaque.
69.   - `#[verifier::external_trait_specification]` for `TableEntry` (`ExTableEntry`,
70.     `: Copy`).
71.   - `assume_specification` (no `requires`/`ensures` — state-free placeholders) for
72.     `pd_index`, `pt_index`, `Table::<E>::from_address`, `Table::<E>::read`,
73.     `Table::<E>::write`, plus `invlpg`.
74. - Functions WITHOUT specs: `TableIndex::new`, `TableIndex::into_raw`,
75.   and the `TableEntry::raw`/`from_raw` trait methods (no external spec; opaque).
76. - View type: **none** — `Table`/`TableIndex` are currently opaque (`external_body`).
77. 
78. ### Assessment
79. 
80. - **Coverage:** partial. Only the functions the identity-map walker needed are
81.   given boundary specs; `into_raw`/`new` and the `raw`/`from_raw` trait methods
82.   are unspecified.
83. - **Strength:** weak — the `assume_specification`s are state-free with no
84.   `ensures`, and the corresponding obligations in the exec bodies are
85.   `admit()`-ed (`ensure_pte`, `ensure_pt`, etc.). They exist only to let the
86.   identity-map bodies translate, not to prove anything about table contents.
87. - **View design:** absent / biased. There is no abstract `View` yet; `Table` is
88.   fully opaque. A real View must model a table as a finite map
89.   `TableIndex → Option<E>` so that `read` after `write` can be reasoned about —
90.   the current opaque placeholder cannot express the read/write round-trip the
91.   identity map relies on.
92. 
93. ## Trait Obligations
94. 
95. - **Trait `TableEntry: Copy`** — semantics expected by `Table`:
96.   - `from_raw(raw) -> Option<Self>`: parse a raw `PteWord` (`u32`), returning
97.     `None` exactly for raw values that are not a valid encoding of `E`.
98.   - `raw(self) -> PteWord`: serialize back to the raw word.
99.   - Round-trip expectation from callers: an entry built via `E::new(...)` and
100.     written, then read back, must yield `Some(equivalent entry)`; an
101.     all-zero / not-present word read by the identity map is a *valid* entry
102.     (returns `Some`, with `is_present() == false`) — `None` denotes structural
103.     corruption, which callers surface as `InvalidArgument`.
104.   - `Copy` lets `write` take `entry` by value and `read` return it freely.
105. 
106. ## Caller Expectations
107. 
108. ### `pd_index(vaddr) -> TableIndex`
109. - Callers assume: returns the PD index = `(vaddr >> PGTAB_SHIFT) &
110.   (PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH - 1)`, always in `[0, PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH)`. Total (no panic,
111.   no failure) for any `usize`. `const`.
112. - Callers don't care about: how the bits are masked, or that the result wraps an
113.   internal `usize` — only that `into_raw()` of it equals the masked value.
114. 
115. ### `pt_index(vaddr) -> TableIndex`
116. - Callers assume: returns the PT index = `(vaddr >> PAGE_SHIFT) &
117.   (PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH - 1)`, always in range; total; `const`.
118. - Callers don't care about: internal representation.
119. 
120. ### `TableIndex` (type) / `TableIndex::into_raw(self) -> usize`
121. - Callers assume: a `TableIndex` is a *validated* index, guaranteed
122.   `< PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH`; `into_raw` is the identity projection back to that
123.   validated `usize` (loss-less, total, `const`). `gva.rs` multiplies it by entry
124.   size with `checked_mul`, relying on the bound to stay within a page.
125. - Callers don't care about: that it is a newtype over `usize`; only the in-range
126.   invariant and the round-trip with the index extractors matter.
127. 
128. ### `Table::from_address(base) -> Table<E>` (`unsafe`, `const`)
129. - Callers assume: produces a typed, non-owning handle over the page at physical/
130.   identity-mapped `base`; cheap, infallible, side-effect-free. The caller carries
131.   the safety obligation (`base` page-aligned, mapped, readable/writable).
132. - Callers don't care about: that the struct stores only `base` + a `PhantomData`
133.   marker; they care that the phantom type `E` is threaded so PD/PT handles can't
134.   be confused.
135. 
136. ### `Table::read(&self, index) -> Option<E>` (`unsafe`)
137. - Callers assume: volatile-reads the word at `base + index*4` and decodes it via
138.   `E::from_raw`; `Some(e)` for a valid encoding, `None` for an invalid one. Does
139.   not mutate the table. The validated `index` guarantees in-bounds access.
140. - Callers don't care about: the volatile-read mechanism or the `<<
141.   PTE_WORD_SIZE_LOG2` offset math — only the index→entry mapping and the `None`
142.   = "invalid entry" contract (which they map to `InvalidArgument`).
143. 
144. ### `Table::write(&self, index, entry)` (`unsafe`)
145. - Callers assume: volatile-writes `entry.raw()` to `base + index*4`, so that a
146.   subsequent `read(index)` observes `Some(entry)` (read-after-write round-trip).
147.   Only the targeted slot changes. The validated `index` keeps the write in
148.   bounds of the page.
149. - Callers don't care about: the volatile mechanism or offset computation.
150. 
151. ### `TableEntry::from_raw` / `TableEntry::raw`
152. - No direct external callers; invoked only inside `read`/`write`. Expectation is
153.   the round-trip described under *Trait Obligations*.
154. 
155. ## Abstract Resource
156. 
157. This module manages a **single hardware page-table page** as a fixed-length array
158. of `PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH` typed entries, addressed by a *validated* in-range index
159. (`TableIndex`) and accessed by raw base address. Abstractly it is a partial map
160. `TableIndex → Option<E>` over volatile memory the caller owns, plus the pure
161. helpers that derive the PD/PT index of a virtual address.
162. 
163. ## Key Invariants (caller perspective)
164. 
165. - **Index validity:** every `TableIndex` (whether from `pd_index`, `pt_index`, or
166.   `new`) satisfies `into_raw() < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH`; this bound is what keeps
167.   `read`/`write` (and `gva.rs`'s `checked_mul`) within one page.
168. - **Index extraction correctness:** `pd_index`/`pt_index` return exactly the
169.   masked/shifted bit-field of `vaddr`, and `into_raw` returns that same value.
170. - **Read/write round-trip:** `write(i, e)` followed by `read(i)` yields
171.   `Some(e')` with `e'` decoding-equivalent to `e`; writes touch only slot `i`.

 2 types (`Table`, `TableIndex`)** and — importantly — **0 external callers for
 every public function** (only internal callers of `TableIndex::into_raw` from

 > This module lives under `src/libs/arch/src/x86/` — the **32-bit x86** build.
 > rust-analyzer (and thus the script) indexes the **x86_64 host** configuration,
 > so all real call sites — which are compiled only under `cfg(target_arch =
 > "x86")` (kernel) or are host-side software page-walkers — are invisible to the
 > LSP. A textual search across the workspace recovers the true callers below.
 > Treat the script's "no external callers" warning as a configuration artifact,
 > **not** as evidence of dead code.
 
 In-scope (verification-order) functions: `Table::write`, `TableIndex::into_raw`,
 `raw`, `Table::read`, `from_raw`, `pt_index`, `TableIndex`, `pd_index`,
 `Table::from_address`. (`raw`/`from_raw` are the `TableEntry` trait methods,
 implemented in `pde.rs`/`pte.rs` and dispatched only inside `Table::read`/`write`.)
 
 ## Real Callers (recovered by source search)
 
 ### 1. Kernel identity map — `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/identity_map.rs` (primary consumer)
 
 This is the canonical user of the whole module. It walks/builds the kernel's
 two-level identity map:
 
 - `paging::pd_index(vaddr)` / `paging::pt_index(vaddr)` → `TableIndex`
   (L131, L306, L728, L729, L783, L848).
 - `unsafe { Table::<PageDirectoryEntry>::from_address(pd_paddr) }` and
   `Table::<PageTableEntry>::from_address(pt_paddr)` to obtain a typed view over a
   physical (identity-mapped) page (L133, L297, L299, L732, L736, L785, L852, L863).
 - `unsafe { pd.read(pde_idx) }` / `pt.read(pte_idx)` returning
   `Option<PageDirectoryEntry>` / `Option<PageTableEntry>`; callers treat `None`
   as "invalid entry" → `ErrorCode::InvalidArgument` (L308, L316, L535, L633,
   L786, L853, L864).
 - `unsafe { pd.write(pde_idx, new_pde) }` / `pt.write(pte_idx, new_pte)` to
   install freshly-built entries (L320, L583, L665).
 - The entry-type parameter `E` is fixed per level: PD tables only carry
   `PageDirectoryEntry`, PT tables only `PageTableEntry`. The phantom-typed
   `Table<E>` is exactly what enforces this at the call sites.
 
 ### 2. UserVM guest page walker — `src/uservm/src/guest_profiler/gva.rs` (host-side)
 
 `translate_gva()` performs a *software* two-level walk over guest memory:
 
 ```rust
 let pd_index: usize = paging::pd_index(gva as usize).into_raw();
 let pt_index: usize = paging::pt_index(gva as usize).into_raw();
 ```
 
 Here only `pd_index`/`pt_index` and `TableIndex::into_raw` are used; the table
 bytes are read directly from a host pointer (`read_unaligned`) rather than via
 `Table::read`, because the guest's memory is not mapped into the host address
 space. This caller relies *solely* on the index-extraction arithmetic being
 correct (mask to `[0, PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH)`) and on `into_raw` returning that same
 value unchanged.

 - **Source:** added while verifying the kernel `mm::virt::identity_map` module.
 - **File:** `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/identity_map.spec.rs`.

     `pd_index`, `pt_index`, `Table::<E>::from_address`, `Table::<E>::read`,
     `Table::<E>::write`, plus `invlpg`.

   and the `TableEntry::raw`/`from_raw` trait methods (no external spec; opaque).

 - **Coverage:** partial. Only the functions the identity-map walker needed are
   given boundary specs; `into_raw`/`new` and the `raw`/`from_raw` trait methods
   are unspecified.
 - **Strength:** weak — the `assume_specification`s are state-free with no
   `ensures`, and the corresponding obligations in the exec bodies are
   `admit()`-ed (`ensure_pte`, `ensure_pt`, etc.). They exist only to let the
   identity-map bodies translate, not to prove anything about table contents.
 - **View design:** absent / biased. There is no abstract `View` yet; `Table` is
   fully opaque. A real View must model a table as a finite map
   `TableIndex → Option<E>` so that `read` after `write` can be reasoned about —
   the current opaque placeholder cannot express the read/write round-trip the
   identity map relies on.
 
 ## Trait Obligations
 
 - **Trait `TableEntry: Copy`** — semantics expected by `Table`:
   - `from_raw(raw) -> Option<Self>`: parse a raw `PteWord` (`u32`), returning
     `None` exactly for raw values that are not a valid encoding of `E`.
   - `raw(self) -> PteWord`: serialize back to the raw word.
   - Round-trip expectation from callers: an entry built via `E::new(...)` and
     written, then read back, must yield `Some(equivalent entry)`; an
     all-zero / not-present word read by the identity map is a *valid* entry
     (returns `Some`, with `is_present() == false`) — `None` denotes structural
     corruption, which callers surface as `InvalidArgument`.
   - `Copy` lets `write` take `entry` by value and `read` return it freely.
 
 ## Caller Expectations
 
 ### `pd_index(vaddr) -> TableIndex`
 - Callers assume: returns the PD index = `(vaddr >> PGTAB_SHIFT) &
   (PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH - 1)`, always in `[0, PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH)`. Total (no panic,
   no failure) for any `usize`. `const`.
 - Callers don't care about: how the bits are masked, or that the result wraps an
   internal `usize` — only that `into_raw()` of it equals the masked value.
 
 ### `pt_index(vaddr) -> TableIndex`
 - Callers assume: returns the PT index = `(vaddr >> PAGE_SHIFT) &
   (PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH - 1)`, always in range; total; `const`.
 - Callers don't care about: internal representation.
 
 ### `TableIndex` (type) / `TableIndex::into_raw(self) -> usize`
 - Callers assume: a `TableIndex` is a *validated* index, guaranteed
   `< PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH`; `into_raw` is the identity projection back to that
   validated `usize` (loss-less, total, `const`). `gva.rs` multiplies it by entry
   size with `checked_mul`, relying on the bound to stay within a page.
 - Callers don't care about: that it is a newtype over `usize`; only the in-range
   invariant and the round-trip with the index extractors matter.
 
 ### `Table::from_address(base) -> Table<E>` (`unsafe`, `const`)
 - Callers assume: produces a typed, non-owning handle over the page at physical/
   identity-mapped `base`; cheap, infallible, side-effect-free. The caller carries
   the safety obligation (`base` page-aligned, mapped, readable/writable).
 - Callers don't care about: that the struct stores only `base` + a `PhantomData`
   marker; they care that the phantom type `E` is threaded so PD/PT handles can't
   be confused.
 
 ### `Table::read(&self, index) -> Option<E>` (`unsafe`)
 - Callers assume: volatile-reads the word at `base + index*4` and decodes it via
   `E::from_raw`; `Some(e)` for a valid encoding, `None` for an invalid one. Does
   not mutate the table. The validated `index` guarantees in-bounds access.
 - Callers don't care about: the volatile-read mechanism or the `<<
   PTE_WORD_SIZE_LOG2` offset math — only the index→entry mapping and the `None`
   = "invalid entry" contract (which they map to `InvalidArgument`).
 
 ### `Table::write(&self, index, entry)` (`unsafe`)
 - Callers assume: volatile-writes `entry.raw()` to `base + index*4`, so that a
   subsequent `read(index)` observes `Some(entry)` (read-after-write round-trip).
   Only the targeted slot changes. The validated `index` keeps the write in
   bounds of the page.
 - Callers don't care about: the volatile mechanism or offset computation.
 
 ### `TableEntry::from_raw` / `TableEntry::raw`
 - No direct external callers; invoked only inside `read`/`write`. Expectation is
   the round-trip described under *Trait Obligations*.
 
 ## Abstract Resource
 
 This module manages a **single hardware page-table page** as a fixed-length array
 of `PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH` typed entries, addressed by a *validated* in-range index
 (`TableIndex`) and accessed by raw base address. Abstractly it is a partial map
 `TableIndex → Option<E>` over volatile memory the caller owns, plus the pure
 helpers that derive the PD/PT index of a virtual address.
 
 ## Key Invariants (caller perspective)
 
 - **Index validity:** every `TableIndex` (whether from `pd_index`, `pt_index`, or
   `new`) satisfies `into_raw() < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH`; this bound is what keeps
   `read`/`write` (and `gva.rs`'s `checked_mul`) within one page.
 - **Index extraction correctness:** `pd_index`/`pt_index` return exactly the
   masked/shifted bit-field of `vaddr`, and `into_raw` returns that same value.
 - **Read/write round-trip:** `write(i, e)` followed by `read(i)` yields
   `Some(e')` with `e'` decoding-equivalent to `e`; writes touch only slot `i`.
 - **Decode totality:** `read` returns `None` only for raw words that are not a
   valid `E` encoding; a not-present (zeroed) entry is a valid `Some`, not `None`.
 - **Type discipline:** `Table<E>`'s phantom `E` prevents mixing PD and PT entries
   across table levels — a property callers depend on but that has no runtime cost.
 - **Non-ownership:** `from_address` does not allocate or free; lifetime/validity
   of the backing page is the caller's responsibility (encoded as `unsafe`).

name: verus-constraints
description: "Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code."
---

# Verus Constraints

## Attribute Style for Exec Functions

All specs on **exec functions** must use the attribute-based syntax
(`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`).
See the **verus-syntax** skill for the full reference and examples.

```rust
// ✅ CORRECT — attribute style for exec functions
#[verus_spec(ret =>
    requires x < 100,
    ensures ret == x + 1,
)]
fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 {
    x + 1
}

// ❌ WRONG — do not wrap exec functions in verus! { }
verus! {
    fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
        requires x < 100,
        ensures ret == x + 1,
    { x + 1 }
} // verus!
```

**`verus! { }` blocks** are still used for:
- `spec fn` and `proof fn` definitions (in `.spec.rs` and `.proof.rs`)
- Type-level specs (`broadcast`, `impl View`, etc.)

Key benefit: exec function signatures stay unmodified — the original `fn`
signature is untouched, specs live in the attribute.

## Source Integrity (exec code)

The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
`*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.

Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Keep changes
minimal so developers can review diffs easily.

**Preserve by default:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions,
comments, debug assertions, and all other existing code.

The escalation ladder (each step requires exhausting the previous):

1. **Verify as-is** — most code works with Verus directly.
2. **Search vstd** — your training data is likely outdated. `grep -r` the entire
   vstd directory broadly (see "vstd & Common Misconceptions" section below).
3. If verification still fails after steps 1–2, try different proof
   strategies (add lemmas, intermediate assertions, split into smaller
   functions). If Verus reports that a **syntax construct is unsupported**
   (not a proof failure and not a missing spec for a stdlib function),
   record it in `verus-unsupported.md` with the exact error message and
   the minimal code that triggers it. Do NOT rewrite exec code, add
   `external_body`, or add `assume_specification` to work around it.

**The exec code has been pre-refactored to be fully compatible with Verus.**
There are no known Verus front-end limitations in the codebase. Any
verification failure is a proof issue, not a Verus limitation. Do NOT
rewrite exec code, add `external_body` — these are never needed.

**Never cfg-gate away and duplicate exec definitions.** Adding
`#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to a function, impl block, struct, enum, or
constant and providing a verus-annotated copy is forbidden — it verifies the
copy, not the real code, and the two will silently diverge.

- **Functions / impl blocks**: add contracts to the original in-place.
- **Structs / enums**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If a
  derive macro is incompatible, cfg-gate only the derive attribute, not
  the struct. If the struct truly cannot be parsed by Verus, use
  `external_type_specification` in spec.rs to declare it — do not
  duplicate the definition. Write `external_type_specification` **once**
  in the crate/module that defines the type; other modules `use` it.
- **Constants**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If Verus
  cannot resolve a constant from another workspace module, add
  `#[verus_verify]` to the defining module. Never
  `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` the original constant.

**Allowed additions:** `#[verus_spec(...)]` and `#[verus_verify]` attributes,
`proof! { }` / `proof_decl! { }` / `proof_with! { }` macros, `#[verus_spec(...)]`
on loops, `verus! { }` blocks (for spec/proof fn in .spec.rs/.proof.rs),
vstd imports (cfg-gated), ghost/tracked local variables (each must be
used by at least one proof construct — assertion, invariant, or proof block),
`Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` struct fields (only when proof requires ghost
state to flow through exec code — prefer keeping ghost state in View),
`#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]` gating.

**After completing all changes**, use the `ast-consistency` skill to verify
source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies.

## Forbidden Patterns

| Pattern | Policy |
|---|---|
| `admit()` | Allowed during specification phase as a placeholder. Must be eliminated during proving phase |
| `assume(...)` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external_body]` | **On current module's own functions**: unconditionally forbidden in all phases — `admit()` in a proof body is the correct placeholder during specification (it skips only the proof obligation while Verus still checks exec code; `external_body` skips everything). **On dependency functions in other modules**: allowed as a temporary contract placeholder while the dependency is not yet verified. Must be removed when the dependency module is verified |
| `#[verifier::trusted]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external]` | Banned — not needed under attribute style (only `#[verus_verify]`-annotated items are checked) |
| `#[verifier::exec_allows_no_decreases_clause]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::spinoff_prover]` | Banned — even if verification passes with spinoff, the proof is fragile and will break with minor changes. Improve the proof itself |
| `#[verifier::rlimit(N)]` | Timeout means the proof is too weak — simplify the proof, split lemmas, add intermediate assertions. Never use rlimit to work around timeouts. If all proof strategies are exhausted and the proof is genuinely optimal, rlimit up to 50 is the absolute maximum |
| `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` on exec code | **Cheating** — cfg-gating branches, expressions, match arms, or code blocks means Verus verifies different code than what runs. Only allowed on non-semantic items: `derive(...)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`), and imports |
| `uninterp spec fn` | **Banned** — all spec functions must have concrete definitions. Using `uninterp` to avoid writing a concrete spec is cheating — it has the same effect as `assume` when paired with `external_body` proof axioms |

## cfg_attr and verus_keep_ghost

- **Do NOT wrap any Verus attribute or proof macro in `cfg_attr(verus_keep_ghost, ...)`, and do NOT guard one with `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]`.** This applies to `#[verus_spec(...)]`, `#[verus_verify(...)]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`, and `proof_with! { }`. These constructs are *already ghost*: the macros erase themselves during a normal (non-Verus) `cargo build` and only take effect under `verus_keep_ghost`, so an extra `verus_keep_ghost` gate is redundant and wrong. Write them directly.
- **`use vstd::prelude::*;` must NOT be cfg-gated** — do not add `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]`. This import must be unconditionally present so that Verus-specific constructs (e.g. `#[verus_spec]`, `proof!{}`) are properly parsed and erased during normal `cargo build`.

See **verus-syntax** skill for correct examples.

name: ast-consistency
description: "AST-level exec fidelity checking tools and pre-approved deviations. Use after modifying source files to verify exec code is unchanged."
---

# AST Consistency Check

Source exec code must not change during verification — see `verus-constraints`
for the full rules. This skill covers the **tooling** to enforce that guarantee.

## Tools

The checker uses tree-sitter to hash exec code after stripping all
ghost/proof/spec annotations. It detects changes invisible to textual diff.

`scripts/ast_consistency.py` provides four subcommands:
- `count` — quick pass/fail
- `summary` — per-element status table
- `diff --name "Fn::name"` — unified diff for one function/struct
- `report -o <dir>` — full report with all diffs

The `source` argument is optional. Use `--base-ref` to extract the original
from git, or omit both on `verus-ai/*` branches for auto-detection:

```bash
# Explicit original file:
python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py original.rs verified.rs count

# Via git ref:
python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py --base-ref main verified.rs count

# Auto-detect on verus-ai/* branches:
python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py verified.rs count
```

`diff` with `--full` shows specs; default is exec-only.

**MCP alternative**: If the `verus-ast` MCP server is registered, the same
functionality is available as tools (`ast_count`, `ast_summary`, `ast_diff`,
`ast_report`) with the same auto-detection.

## Pre-Approved Deviations

These minimal exec changes are known Verus limitations — no full deviation
process needed, but still document with a comment:

| Original | Verus Version | Reason |
|----------|--------------|--------|
| `self.x += 1` | `self.x = self.x + 1` | Compound assignment unsupported |
| `self.arr[i] \|= v` | `self.arr.set(i, self.arr[i] \| v)` | Mutable index unsupported |
| `-> T` | `-> (ret: T)` | Named returns for ensures |
| `#[derive(Clone, ...)]` | `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))] #[derive(...)]` | cfg-gating incompatible derives |
| `Ok(Self { .. })` | `let result = Self { .. }; Ok(result)` | Ensures needs to reference return value |
| `f(complex_expr)` | `let x = complex_expr; f(x)` | Intermediate value for assertions |
| `.ok_or_else(\|\| ...)` | `match ... { Some(v) => v, None => return Err(...) }` | Closures unsupported in some contexts |
| `v.std_method(args)` | `wrapper(&mut v, args)` | `&mut T` method unsupported; see `verus-constraints` skill for wrapper rules |

### Bug Fix Deviations

Exec changes that fix verified bugs are also pre-approved. These must:
- Have a `// VERUS BUG FIX: <description>` comment at the fix site
- Be recorded in `bugs.md` with full evidence
- Be committed with `[verus-ai] BUG FIX:` prefix
- Be limited to auto-fixable categories (overflow, off-by-one, missing
  bounds check, unchecked cast) — see `bug-reporting` skill

## Handling MISMATCHes

When the checker reports a MISMATCH:

1. **Default: restore original code.** Exec changes are violations. Use
   `git show <base_ref>:path/to/file.rs` to view the original, then
   manually restore the changed exec code while keeping your annotations.
   Adapt the proof to the original code — not the other way around.
2. **Check pre-approved deviations.** If the change matches one above,
   keep it but add a comment documenting which deviation and why.
3. **Verify it's a real Verus limitation.** Before accepting any other
   change, confirm Verus genuinely cannot handle the original construct:
   - Search vstd for existing support (e.g. `checked_mul` has vstd specs)
   - Try alternative proof strategies that preserve the original code

Source exec code must not change during verification — see `verus-constraints`
for the full rules. This skill covers the **tooling** to enforce that guarantee.

## Tools

The checker uses tree-sitter to hash exec code after stripping all
ghost/proof/spec annotations. It detects changes invisible to textual diff.

`scripts/ast_consistency.py` provides four subcommands:
- `count` — quick pass/fail
- `summary` — per-element status table
- `diff --name "Fn::name"` — unified diff for one function/struct
- `report -o <dir>` — full report with all diffs

The `source` argument is optional. Use `--base-ref` to extract the original
from git, or omit both on `verus-ai/*` branches for auto-detection:

```bash
# Explicit original file:
python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py original.rs verified.rs count

# Via git ref:
python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py --base-ref main verified.rs count

# Auto-detect on verus-ai/* branches:
python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py verified.rs count
```

`diff` with `--full` shows specs; default is exec-only.

**MCP alternative**: If the `verus-ast` MCP server is registered, the same
functionality is available as tools (`ast_count`, `ast_summary`, `ast_diff`,
`ast_report`) with the same auto-detection.

## Pre-Approved Deviations

These minimal exec changes are known Verus limitations — no full deviation
process needed, but still document with a comment:

| Original | Verus Version | Reason |
|----------|--------------|--------|
| `self.x += 1` | `self.x = self.x + 1` | Compound assignment unsupported |
| `self.arr[i] \|= v` | `self.arr.set(i, self.arr[i] \| v)` | Mutable index unsupported |
| `-> T` | `-> (ret: T)` | Named returns for ensures |
| `#[derive(Clone, ...)]` | `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))] #[derive(...)]` | cfg-gating incompatible derives |
| `Ok(Self { .. })` | `let result = Self { .. }; Ok(result)` | Ensures needs to reference return value |
| `f(complex_expr)` | `let x = complex_expr; f(x)` | Intermediate value for assertions |
| `.ok_or_else(\|\| ...)` | `match ... { Some(v) => v, None => return Err(...) }` | Closures unsupported in some contexts |
| `v.std_method(args)` | `wrapper(&mut v, args)` | `&mut T` method unsupported; see `verus-constraints` skill for wrapper rules |

### Bug Fix Deviations

Exec changes that fix verified bugs are also pre-approved. These must:
- Have a `// VERUS BUG FIX: <description>` comment at the fix site
- Be recorded in `bugs.md` with full evidence
- Be committed with `[verus-ai] BUG FIX:` prefix
- Be limited to auto-fixable categories (overflow, off-by-one, missing
  bounds check, unchecked cast) — see `bug-reporting` skill

## Handling MISMATCHes

When the checker reports a MISMATCH:

1. **Default: restore original code.** Exec changes are violations. Use
   `git show <base_ref>:path/to/file.rs` to view the original, then
   manually restore the changed exec code while keeping your annotations.
   Adapt the proof to the original code — not the other way around.
2. **Check pre-approved deviations.** If the change matches one above,
   keep it but add a comment documenting which deviation and why.
3. **Verify it's a real Verus limitation.** Before accepting any other
   change, confirm Verus genuinely cannot handle the original construct:
   - Search vstd for existing support (e.g. `checked_mul` has vstd specs)
   - Try alternative proof strategies that preserve the original code

# Spec Design Guide

## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles

### Qualities of a Good Spec

1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
   `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
   functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
   exec function using `#[verus_spec]` (see `verus-syntax` skill). Never
   copy exec functions into a `verus!{}` block and spec the copy — that
   verifies the copy, not the real code.
3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
   that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
   that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
   not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
   bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
5. **Simpler than the code** — the spec should be at a higher level of
   abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
   loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
   recursive spec functions.
6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
   If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
   test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
   type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
   If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
   over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
   `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state. For pointer
   addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
   non-negative and bounded by the address space.
8. **Written for the caller** — for each ensures clause, simulate
   writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
   this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
   unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
   directly into their proof. Prefer vstd's existing spec functions
   (e.g., `self@.contains(x)`) over manual encodings (e.g.,
   `exists|i| ... && self@[i] == x`) — callers already reason with
   vstd APIs. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely hides
   implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from inputs
   and return values through the module's public spec interface,
   `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.

### Exec Binding Rules — Desk Reject Criteria

If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in
spec.rs/proof.rs. Our goal is a **verified implementation**, not a verified
design model.

1. **Every exec function in scope gets contracts** — "in scope" is determined
   by the verification task (e.g., caller analysis, human directive, or
   module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public

---
name: bug-reporting
description: "Classify and report bugs found during Verus verification. Distinguishes true bugs from missing constraints and verifier limitations. Use when a verification failure might indicate a code bug."
---

# Bug Reporting

Finding real code bugs is a high-value outcome of formal verification.
Not every verification failure is a bug — ensure you have genuinely attempted
to prove it first (see `proving-guide`) before classifying a failure as one.

## Classification

After genuinely exhausting proof attempts (see `proving-guide`), classify
every remaining verification failure into one of three categories:

**True Bug** — the code is wrong regardless of calling context. No reasonable
precondition could make it correct (e.g. arithmetic overflow on all inputs,
logic error that always produces wrong results).

**Context-Dependent** — the code looks incorrect in isolation but may be
correct given constraints enforced elsewhere (e.g. callers guarantee bounds,
a system invariant ensures uniqueness). Check callers, upstream module specs,
and system-wide invariants before concluding it's a bug.

**False Positive** — the code is correct but verification fails due to
spec errors (overly strong postcondition, wrong invariant) or solver
limitations (trigger issues, quantifier reasoning gaps).

## When to Report

- **True Bug**: report immediately. This is the highest-value finding.
- **Context-Dependent**: report with analysis of what constraints would be
  needed and where they might come from.
- **False Positive**: do not report — fix the proof approach instead.
  Never weaken existing specs (requires/ensures) to work around a verification
  failure; see `verus-constraints`.

## Auto-Fixable Bugs

Some true bugs are mechanical and can be fixed immediately to unblock
verification. **Fix these directly in the source code** and commit with
the `[verus-ai] BUG FIX:` prefix so the fix is clearly attributed to
verification. Still record them in `bugs.md`.

Auto-fixable categories:
- **Arithmetic overflow/underflow**: missing checked arithmetic or bounds
  checks (e.g. `a + b` → `a.checked_add(b)`, or adding a bounds guard)
- **Off-by-one**: fencepost errors in loop bounds or index calculations
- **Missing bounds check**: index used without prior length/capacity check
- **Unchecked cast**: lossy `as` cast without range validation

For each auto-fix:
1. Make the **minimal** code change that fixes the bug
2. Record the fix in `bugs.md` with full details (see Report Format)
3. Add `// VERUS BUG FIX: <one-line description>` comment at the fix site
4. Re-run AST consistency — the fix is a **pre-approved deviation** (bug fix category)
5. Commit with `git commit --no-verify -m "[verus-ai] BUG FIX: <description>"` message
   (`--no-verify` is required because pre-commit hooks would reject exec changes)

Do NOT auto-fix:
- Algorithmic/design bugs (wrong data structure, incorrect state machine logic)
- Concurrency bugs (race conditions, missing synchronization)
- Anything requiring architectural changes
- Anything where the "fix" is unclear or has multiple valid approaches

For these, report only — a human should decide.

## Report Format

1. # View Design: `arch::x86::mem::paging::table`
2. 
3. ## Abstract Resource
4. 
5. To callers this module is **a single hardware page-table page**: a fixed-length
6. array of `PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH` (= 1024) typed entries, addressed by a *validated*
7. in-range index (`TableIndex`) and backed by volatile, caller-owned memory at a
8. physical/identity-mapped base address.
9. 
10. Abstractly it is a **partial map `index → Option<E>`** over one page, plus two
11. pure helpers (`pd_index`, `pt_index`) that extract the directory/table index of
12. a virtual address. The phantom type `E` keeps PD and PT pages from being mixed.
13. 
14. Two types need abstraction:
15. 
16. | Type | What it is to a caller |
17. |------|------------------------|
18. | `TableIndex` | a *validated* slot number, guaranteed `< PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH` |
19. | `Table<E>` | a typed, non-owning handle whose observable content is the per-slot entry map |
20. 
21. ---
22. 
23. ## View Structs
24. 
25. ### `TableIndex`
26. 
27. A `TableIndex` carries exactly one piece of caller-visible information: the
28. validated index value. Its abstract value is a single `nat`.
29. 
30. ```rust
31. impl View for TableIndex {
32.     type V = nat;
33.     // value returned by into_raw(); always < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH (see inv)
34.     pub closed spec fn view(&self) -> nat;
35. }
36. ```
37. 
38. ### `Table<E>`
39. 
40. ```rust
41. pub struct TableView<E: TableEntry> {
42.     /// Physical/identity-mapped base address this handle denotes.
43.     /// Caller-meaningful identity: which page read/write act on.
44.     pub addr: nat,
45.     /// Logical contents: the entry a `read` would return for each valid slot.
46.     /// `entries[i] == None` means slot `i` holds a word that is not a valid
47.     /// encoding of `E`; `Some(e)` (including a not-present, zeroed entry) is a
48.     /// valid decode.
49.     pub entries: Map<nat, Option<E>>,
50. }
51. 
52. impl View for Table<E> {
53.     type V = TableView<E>;
54.     pub closed spec fn view(&self) -> TableView<E>;
55. }
56. ```
57. 
58. `E: TableEntry` is `Copy`; the trait supplies two pure spec projections used by
59. the transitions below (their `requires`/`ensures` are designed in the spec
60. phase; `raw`/`from_raw` are in verification scope, so these are *proven*, not
61. assumed):
62. 
63. ```rust
64. spec fn spec_raw(self: E) -> PteWord;              // serialize
65. spec fn spec_from_raw(w: PteWord) -> Option<E>;    // decode (None = invalid)
66. ```
67. 
68. with the round-trip **trait law** `spec_from_raw(e.spec_raw()) == Some(e)`.
69. 
70. ---
71. 
72. ## Well-formedness Invariants
73. 
74. ```rust
75. // TableIndex: the validated-range guarantee callers depend on.
76. pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {     // on TableIndex
77.     self@ < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH
78. }
79. ```
80.

 | Type | What it is to a caller |
 |------|------------------------|
 | `TableIndex` | a *validated* slot number, guaranteed `< PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH` |
 | `Table<E>` | a typed, non-owning handle whose observable content is the per-slot entry map |
 
 ---
 
 ## View Structs
 
 ### `TableIndex`
 
 A `TableIndex` carries exactly one piece of caller-visible information: the
 validated index value. Its abstract value is a single `nat`.
 
 ```rust
 impl View for TableIndex {
     type V = nat;
     // value returned by into_raw(); always < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH (see inv)
     pub closed spec fn view(&self) -> nat;
 }
 ```
 
 ### `Table<E>`
 
 ```rust
 pub struct TableView<E: TableEntry> {
     /// Physical/identity-mapped base address this handle denotes.
     /// Caller-meaningful identity: which page read/write act on.
     pub addr: nat,
     /// Logical contents: the entry a `read` would return for each valid slot.
     /// `entries[i] == None` means slot `i` holds a word that is not a valid
     /// encoding of `E`; `Some(e)` (including a not-present, zeroed entry) is a
     /// valid decode.
     pub entries: Map<nat, Option<E>>,
 }
 
 impl View for Table<E> {
     type V = TableView<E>;
     pub closed spec fn view(&self) -> TableView<E>;
 }
 ```
 
 `E: TableEntry` is `Copy`; the trait supplies two pure spec projections used by
 the transitions below (their `requires`/`ensures` are designed in the spec
 phase; `raw`/`from_raw` are in verification scope, so these are *proven*, not
 assumed):
 
 ```rust
 spec fn spec_raw(self: E) -> PteWord;              // serialize
 spec fn spec_from_raw(w: PteWord) -> Option<E>;    // decode (None = invalid)
 ```
 
 with the round-trip **trait law** `spec_from_raw(e.spec_raw()) == Some(e)`.
 
 ---
 
 ## Well-formedness Invariants
 
 ```rust
 // TableIndex: the validated-range guarantee callers depend on.
 pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {     // on TableIndex
     self@ < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH
 }
 ```

 Search broadly across the entire vstd directory — do not only check one or
 two files. Look in `vstd/std_specs/`, `vstd/seq*.rs`, `vstd/map*.rs`,
 `vstd/set*.rs`, `vstd/arithmetic/`, `vstd/raw_ptr.rs`, etc.
 
 - **Never invent vstd functions** — verify existence in actual vstd source.
 - **Verus supports `for` loops** — do not replace with `while` unless semantically appropriate.
 - **Don't hallucinate syntax** — when unsure, check the Verus reference or vstd examples.
 
 ## Claiming Verus Limitations
 
 **The exec code has been pre-refactored to be fully Verus-compatible.**
 There are no known Verus front-end limitations in the codebase. Do NOT
 claim any construct is unsupported, rewrite exec code, add `external_body`,
 or use `// VERUS REWRITE`. Any verification failure is a proof issue —
 strengthen the proof, do not change the code.
 
 ### Guardrails
 
 **Cfg-gating exec code is cheating.** `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` is only
 appropriate for non-semantic items that Verus truly cannot parse:
 `derive(Debug)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`).
 Do NOT cfg-gate match arms, closures, large code blocks, or expressions.
 This makes Verus verify different code than what actually runs.
 
 **Anti-pattern — body duplication (absolutely forbidden):**
 
 ```rust
 // ❌ WRONG: real body hidden from Verus, replaced with different code
 fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> {
     #[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
     { /* real implementation */ }
     #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
     { /* different code that Verus can parse */ }
 }
 ```
 
 **Anti-pattern — function duplication (absolutely forbidden):**
 
 ```rust
 // ❌ WRONG: entire function gated out, replaced with a different definition
 #[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
 fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> { /* real */ }
 #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
 fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> { /* different */ }
 ```
 
 Both patterns verify a **different program** than what ships. The proof is
 meaningless. Find a single body that both Rust and Verus accept.

2. name: bug-reporting
3. description: "Classify and report bugs found during Verus verification. Distinguishes true bugs from missing constraints and verifier limitations. Use when a verification failure might indicate a code bug."
4. ---
5. 
6. # Bug Reporting
7. 
8. Finding real code bugs is a high-value outcome of formal verification.
9. Not every verification failure is a bug — ensure you have genuinely attempted
10. to prove it first (see `proving-guide`) before classifying a failure as one.
11. 
12. ## Classification
13. 
14. After genuinely exhausting proof attempts (see `proving-guide`), classify
15. every remaining verification failure into one of three categories:
16. 
17. **True Bug** — the code is wrong regardless of calling context. No reasonable
18. precondition could make it correct (e.g. arithmetic overflow on all inputs,
19. logic error that always produces wrong results).
20. 
21. **Context-Dependent** — the code looks incorrect in isolation but may be
22. correct given constraints enforced elsewhere (e.g. callers guarantee bounds,
23. a system invariant ensures uniqueness). Check callers, upstream module specs,
24. and system-wide invariants before concluding it's a bug.
25. 
26. **False Positive** — the code is correct but verification fails due to
27. spec errors (overly strong postcondition, wrong invariant) or solver
28. limitations (trigger issues, quantifier reasoning gaps).
29. 
30. ## When to Report
31. 
32. - **True Bug**: report immediately. This is the highest-value finding.
33. - **Context-Dependent**: report with analysis of what constraints would be
34.   needed and where they might come from.
35. - **False Positive**: do not report — fix the proof approach instead.
36.   Never weaken existing specs (requires/ensures) to work around a verification
37.   failure; see `verus-constraints`.
38. 
39. ## Auto-Fixable Bugs
40. 
41. Some true bugs are mechanical and can be fixed immediately to unblock
42. verification. **Fix these directly in the source code** and commit with
43. the `[verus-ai] BUG FIX:` prefix so the fix is clearly attributed to
44. verification. Still record them in `bugs.md`.
45. 
46. Auto-fixable categories:
47. - **Arithmetic overflow/underflow**: missing checked arithmetic or bounds
48.   checks (e.g. `a + b` → `a.checked_add(b)`, or adding a bounds guard)
49. - **Off-by-one**: fencepost errors in loop bounds or index calculations
50. - **Missing bounds check**: index used without prior length/capacity check
51. - **Unchecked cast**: lossy `as` cast without range validation
52. 
53. For each auto-fix:
54. 1. Make the **minimal** code change that fixes the bug
55. 2. Record the fix in `bugs.md` with full details (see Report Format)
56. 3. Add `// VERUS BUG FIX: <one-line description>` comment at the fix site
57. 4. Re-run AST consistency — the fix is a **pre-approved deviation** (bug fix category)
58. 5. Commit with `git commit --no-verify -m "[verus-ai] BUG FIX: <description>"` message
59.    (`--no-verify` is required because pre-commit hooks would reject exec changes)
60. 
61. Do NOT auto-fix:
62. - Algorithmic/design bugs (wrong data structure, incorrect state machine logic)
63. - Concurrency bugs (race conditions, missing synchronization)
64. - Anything requiring architectural changes
65. - Anything where the "fix" is unclear or has multiple valid approaches
66. 
67. For these, report only — a human should decide.
68. 
69. ## Report Format
70. 
71. Write findings to the bugs file (path provided in prompt context).
72. Reports will be read by human developers — use clear language, avoid jargon,
73. and make each report self-contained so readers need no additional context.
74. 
75. ```markdown
76. ## [True Bug | Context-Dependent] — function_name (file.rs:line)
77. 
78. **What**: one-line summary of the issue.
79. **Why**: root cause analysis — what the code does wrong and why.
80. **Verification Failure**: which clause failed (requires/ensures/invariant/assert),
81. verification command, and key error output.
82. **How Verus Helped**: how formal verification caught this bug (e.g. would it
83. be caught by testing? code review? why verification was uniquely effective).
84. **Severity**: safety-critical / correctness / cosmetic.
85. **Suggested Fix**: how the code should be changed.
86. **Auto-Fixed**: Yes/No — if yes, describe the exact change made.
87. ```
88. 
89. If no bugs are found, write "None" to the bugs file.
90.

2. name: spec-design
3. description: "How to write good Verus specs. Covers spec quality principles (anti-patterns, error paths), spec classification (internal, external-top, external-bottom trust boundaries), View abstraction design, and static vs dynamic enforcement. Use when writing or reviewing Verus specs."
4. ---
5. 
6. # Spec Design Guide
7. 
8. ## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles
9. 
10. ### Qualities of a Good Spec
11. 
12. 1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
13.    `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
14.    functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
15. 2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
16.    exec function using `#[verus_spec]` (see `verus-syntax` skill). Never
17.    copy exec functions into a `verus!{}` block and spec the copy — that
18.    verifies the copy, not the real code.
19. 3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
20.    that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
21.    that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
22. 4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
23.    not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
24.    bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
25. 5. **Simpler than the code** — the spec should be at a higher level of
26.    abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
27.    loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
28.    recursive spec functions.
29. 6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
30.    If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
31.    test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
32.    type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
33.    If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
34. 7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
35.    over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
36.    `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state. For pointer
37.    addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
38.    non-negative and bounded by the address space.
39. 8. **Written for the caller** — for each ensures clause, simulate
40.    writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
41.    this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
42.    unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
43.    directly into their proof. Prefer vstd's existing spec functions
44.    (e.g., `self@.contains(x)`) over manual encodings (e.g.,
45.    `exists|i| ... && self@[i] == x`) — callers already reason with
46.    vstd APIs. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely hides
47.    implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from inputs
48.    and return values through the module's public spec interface,
49.    `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.
50. 
51. ### Exec Binding Rules — Desk Reject Criteria
52. 
53. If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
54. nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in
55. spec.rs/proof.rs. Our goal is a **verified implementation**, not a verified
56. design model.
57. 
58. 1. **Every exec function in scope gets contracts** — "in scope" is determined
59.    by the verification task (e.g., caller analysis, human directive, or
60.    module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public
61.    and safety-critical functions. No annotation is a desk reject; partial
62.    annotation beats no annotation.
63. 2. **Search vstd before writing `assume_specification`** — vstd already
64.    provides specs for many std library functions. Only write
65.    `assume_specification` for std library or third-party dependency
66.    functions that vstd does not cover. Never for workspace-internal code.
67.    Always search vstd first.
68. 3. **Reuse dependency specs** — before calling a function from another
69.    module in the project, search for its `.spec.rs`:
70.    `find . -name "*.spec.rs" | head -20`. If the dependency has verified
71.    specs, import and use them directly. If it does not, add `#[verus_spec]`
72.    annotations on the dependency function — do NOT use `assume_specification`
73.    for project-internal code (any crate in the workspace). `assume_specification`
74.    is only for third-party dependencies and std library functions not covered
75.    by vstd.
76.    **Why this works without `admit()`**: `--verify-module M` only verifies
77.    functions in module M. Specs on functions in other modules are treated as
78.    trusted contracts — their bodies are not checked. When those modules are
79.    verified later, the specs become fully proven.
80. 5. **No floating specs** — every spec function and lemma must ultimately
81.    connect to an exec contract. Orphan specs are dead code.
82. 6. **No `external_body` on current module** — the current module's functions
83.    must never be marked `external_body`. Use `admit()` in proof bodies to
84.    make Verus pass.
85.    **Dependency functions** in other modules may be marked `external_body`
86.    with `requires`/`ensures` to provide contracts that the current module
87.    can rely on. These are removed when the dependency module is verified.
88.
